articles.title: SpaceX to fly more NASA crews to space station under expanded $5.92 billion deal
articles.summary: Sept 18 (Reuters) - NASA said Friday that the agency had given SpaceX a $946 million contract to fly three more astronaut missions to the International Space...
articles.body:
Sept 18 (Reuters) - NASA said Friday that the agency had given SpaceX a $946 million contract to fly three more astronaut missions ‌to the International Space Station, extending the company's crewed flights to ‌the station through 2030.

The deal brings SpaceX's total number of NASA astronaut flights under the ​contract to 17 and raises the contract's total value to $5.92 billion. NASA is relying heavily on SpaceX to keep astronauts traveling to and from the station while it works to maintain a second U.S. option through Boeing.

The contract ‌covers preparing astronauts and spacecraft ⁠on the ground, launching them, operating the mission in space, bringing crews home and recovering the capsule. It also ⁠includes carrying supplies and keeping the spacecraft at the station as an emergency escape vehicle.

The agency chose SpaceX and Boeing in 2014 to develop spacecraft capable ​of ​carrying astronauts to the space station. The ​goal was to give the ‌United States a regular domestic launch capability after NASA retired the space shuttle, ending years of reliance on Russia's Soyuz spacecraft.

Boeing's Starliner suffered problems on its 2024 crewed test flight, prompting NASA to return the capsule empty and bring astronauts Butch Wilmore and Suni Williams home on a SpaceX ‌Dragon after a planned 10-day mission became ​a more than nine-month ISS stay.

NASA approved SpaceX's ​system for astronaut flights ​in November 2020. Since then, SpaceX has become the agency's ‌main provider for rotating crews at ​the station, using ​its Crew Dragon capsule and Falcon 9 rocket to carry up to four astronauts, as well as supplies.

NASA wants both SpaceX and Boeing ​operating crew flights so ‌that an accident or technical problem affecting one company does ​not halt US astronaut access to the station.

articles.title: Monarch butterflies are heading south. This map shows when they'll pass over you
articles.summary: Cooling weather and changing winds are helping monarch butterflies begin an extraordinary journey of up to 3,000 miles.
articles.body:
An orange-and-black wave is moving south across North America as monarch butterflies embark on one of nature's most remarkable migrations.

As autumn approaches across North America, temperatures fall, daylight fades and milkweed begins to die back. Monarchs born during late summer then begin a journey that can stretch up to 3,000 miles, according to the Xerces Society.

Most monarchs east of the Rocky Mountains fly toward the oyamel fir forests of central Mexico . Many western monarchs migrate toward sheltered groves along the California coast.

Unlike earlier generations, which typically live for only two to six weeks, this migratory "super generation" can survive for up to nine months. The butterflies spend the winter in warmer climates before beginning the return trip north in spring.

The migration begins during August in southern Canada and the northern United States before gradually shifting south through September and October.

Monarch Watch estimates peak abundance around the Great Lakes and portions of the central United States from early to mid-September. The best window shifts toward the central Plains and mid-Atlantic during the second half of September.

Monarch numbers typically peak across parts of the southern Plains and upper parts of the South from late September into early October. The migration reaches the Gulf Coast during October, with many eastern monarchs arriving in central Mexico from late October into November.

The schedule can vary with the weather. Strong southwesterly winds can slow the butterflies' progress, while passing cold fronts and favorable winds from the north or northwest can send large numbers southward.

Monarchs conserve energy by riding air currents and can travel more than 100 miles in a day when conditions are favorable.

Where to look for monarch butterflies during migration

Migrating monarchs fly individually during the day but often gather in trees at night, forming temporary roosts that may contain dozens, hundreds or even thousands of butterflies.

One migration hotspot is northwestern Ohio, where monarchs have recently been spotted in high numbers near Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge. During migration season, the Friends of Ottawa National Wildlife Refuge are hosting monarch hikes around Port Clinton and Oak Harbor , giving visitors a chance to search for the butterflies along their southbound route.

Parks, meadows, wildlife refuges and gardens with abundant late-blooming flowers are among the best places to look. Goldenrod, asters, blazing star, coneflowers and other nectar-rich plants provide critical fuel for the journey.

Sunny mornings and afternoons are generally best for seeing active monarchs, especially after temperatures climb above 55 F. Those hoping to spot a roost should look in sheltered trees during the early morning or near sunset, when the butterflies are more likely to cluster together. Rain, strong winds and chilly conditions can sharply reduce activity.

Monarchs typically begin reaching their winter groves in California during October and remain into early February. The Xerces Society says mid-November through December is usually the best time to see large aggregations at public sites such as Natural Bridges State Beach, Pacific Grove Monarch Sanctuary and Pismo State Beach Monarch Butterfly Grove.

How to help migrating monarchs on their journey

One of the easiest ways to help is to leave late-blooming flowers in place through the first frost. Migrating adults depend on nectar to replenish the energy needed for their long flight.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends planting flowers native to the region that bloom through October. Even a small garden or balcony planter can provide a valuable stopover.

Native milkweed is also essential because it is the only plant on which monarchs lay their eggs and the only food their caterpillars eat. Gardeners should choose milkweed species native to their area and limit the use of pesticides and herbicides.

Observers should avoid touching or handling monarchs and remain on marked paths when visiting overwintering groves. Sightings of wild monarchs and overnight roosts can also be submitted to community science programs such as Journey North, helping researchers track the migration.

The butterflies making this fall's journey have never traveled the route before. Yet, despite being several generations removed from the monarchs that last occupied the winter groves, they can find the same sheltered forests used by their ancestors.

articles.title: FDA approves new breast cancer treatment
articles.summary: The FDA has approved a new breast cancer treatment for patients with advanced and metastatic cancers, such as stage 4.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The FDA has approved a new breast cancer treatment for patients with advanced and metastatic cancers, such as stage 4.

The FDA announced the metastatic cancer treatment option was approved for "adults with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative, estrogen receptor 1 (ESR1)-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer ..." in a news release on Friday.

The pairing of Inluriyo and Verzenio, both oral treatments, was shown to stop cancer from spreading or worsening among those with metastatic cancer for a median of 11.1 months, as opposed to 5.5 months when using Inluriyo alone.

"We have an urgent need for effective and safe treatment options for patients with disease progression on adjuvant or first-line therapy. Combining therapies that work on two distinct drivers of tumor growth... is an important strategy to help address treatment resistance," Komal Jhaveri, MD, FACP, FASCO, principal investigator for the trials, said in a release .

According to the release, Inluriyo contains a warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, and Verzenio contains warnings for severe diarrhea, neutropenia, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, venous thromboembolism, embryo-fetal toxicity, and increased serum creatinine without affecting renal function.

Patients experienced mild to moderate side effects when using the drugs in combination, including diarrhea, nausea, fatigue and decreased white blood cell count, among others.

The FDA noted the recommended dosage of Inluriyo is "400 mg orally once daily (on an empty stomach at least two hours before food or one hour after food)."

The recommended amount of Verzenio in combination with Inluriyo is "150 mg orally twice daily (with or without food) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity."

articles.title: Una familia encuentra en la arena con un detector de metales 51 monedas y una cadena de 12 metros de oro de un naufragio de 1715 con un valor de un millón de euros
articles.standfirst: El suceso tiene lugar en Florida
articles.summary: El suceso tiene lugar en Florida
articles.body: La curiosidad y búsqueda de una familia de Florida, en el año 2015, dio como resultado uno de los hallazgos más curiosos y con un valor increíble, superior al millón de dólares. Al usar un detector de metales en la arena poco profunda, hallaron un botín de 51 monedas de oro y una cadena de 12 metros que corresponden a un naufragio ocurrido en 1715. Este tesoro corresponde a un tesoro español con nada menos que 300 metros de antigüedad y fue encontrado hace una década por la familia Schmitt. El buque protagonista del naufragio fue El Capitán, uno de los más importantes de la flota española en el siglo XVIII. La revista TIME explica que esta familia, especializada en la búsqueda de tesoros y que ejerce como subcontratista para 715 Fleet-Queens Jewels LLC, se topó con una moneda de ocho escudos reales mexicanos llamada ‘Real del Tricentenario’. Al parecer, este buque naufragó cuando se dedicaba a transportar oro, plata y otros productos desde América hasta España. A finales del mes de julio de 1715, la flota española se vio afectada por un huracán que provocó su naufragio en la costa de Florida, junto con otros 10 navíos de los 12 que viajaban a España. Todo el cargamento se perdió en el mar y, desde entonces, buscadores de tesoros han ido tratando de encontrar los restos. Fue en 2013 cuando esta familia encontró por primera vez oro procedente del naufragio, pero ahora su relevancia ha ido a más debido a esa rara moneda de oro, cuyo valor se estima en 500.000 dólares. El resto de las monedas corresponden, en su mayoría, a unas acuñadas en Lima (Perú). El hallazgo se produjo en junio de 2015 cerca de la playa de Fort Pierce, a unos 300 metros y cuando los buzos se movían en una zona de apenas 4,5 metros de profundidad. Ese mismo verano se encontraron otras 350 monedas de oro, demostrando el valor de la mercancía de aquel naufragio.

articles.title: North America loses its monopoly on dinosaur fossils; fourteen tail vertebrae just turned up in Spain and experts have identified it as Diplodocus
articles.summary: Archaeology & Ancient World News: Palaeontologists in Spain have discovered the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils outside of North America, marking the first-ever discovery outside th.
articles.body: Palaeontologists in Spain have discovered the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils outside of North America, marking the first-ever discovery outside the area. For 150 years, every confirmed bone of the animal came from one place, the Morrison Formation of western US. But recently, Sergio Sanchez Fenollosa and his colleagues found the same anatomical signature in a set of tail vertebrae found in Teruel, Spain.The roughly 150-million-year-old remains turned out to be the first confirmed Diplodocus fossils ever found outside North America, the team reported in the Journal of Vertebrate Palaeontology. During the Late Jurassic, falling sea levels may have exposed land that dinosaurs could walk across between the continents. “With each new result, the picture became clearer: we were looking at a Diplodocus,” Sánchez Fenollosa, the study’s lead author, said in a press release.Identifying the first Diplodocus fossilsThe first five vertebrae turned up at La Tejeria back in 2008. It wasn’t until excavations in 2014 and 2015 that the team recovered nine more, along with several chevrons, the bones attached beneath the tail vertebrae. Some of the vertebrae were still connected in the order they’d been in while the animal was alive. The whole find covered roughly 108 square feet (10 square meters).According to Alberto Cobos, one of the study's co-authors, the animal was about 82 feet long. But even that partial tail is among Europe’s most complete finds from the dinosaur’s wider family. Earlier finds from this family in the region included a tooth and scraps of hip and tail bone.Sánchez Fenollosa, Cobos, and co-author Josué García Cobeña measured the bones by hand with callipers or a tape measure and compared them with published descriptions of other long-necked, plant-eating sauropods. The vertebrae had deep grooves running underneath and no ridges along the sides, while the chevrons were forked.The excellent preservation of the specimen allowed the researchers to recognise several anatomical traits associated with Diplodocus, including:Large pneumatic cavities inside the vertebraeDeep longitudinal grooves along the underside of the tail bonesDistinctive forked chevron bones with unique medial fossaeElongated vertebral centra without lateral ridgesThe team recognised that combination in Diplodocus and checked the identification with computer analyses of the animals’ relationships. The results shuffled other parts of the family tree around, but every version placed the Spanish dinosaur on the Diplodocus branch.From North America to SpainDiplodocus now joins Allosaurus and Stegosaurus among dinosaurs from the Jurassic rocks on both sides of the Atlantic. It ranks among the most recognisable dinosaurs ever discovered. It is known for its enormous length (up to 25 meters), long whip-like tail, and relatively small head.Since Diplodocus was first discovered in the United States in 1878, casts of its skeleton have appeared in major natural history museums around the world, particularly during the early 20th century. Those displays helped turn Diplodocus into an international symbol of palaeontology and one of the most familiar dinosaurs in popular culture.At the time these animals lived, the ocean was still opening between the continents. As sea levels fell, stretches of land may have appeared between what’s now Newfoundland and the Iberian Peninsula, home to modern Spain and Portugal. Those temporary routes could have offered animals a way to wander from one continent to the other. However, it still remains unknown to the researchers exactly when Diplodocus crossed between them or which route it took.The team can identify the animal as Diplodocus, but the tail doesn’t preserve enough detail to pin down its species. In their analyses, the Spanish animal came out closest to the North American species Diplodocus hallorum. Finding a more complete skeleton in Europe could help them work out just how closely the two were related.The sediments surrounding the bones were deposited on a coastal plain shaped by rivers. Other enormous plant eaters, including Turiasaurus and Losillasaurus, also lived in what is now Teruel, Cobos notes in the Dinópolis Foundation’s press release. These dinosaurs belonged to a different branch of the sauropod family.The original tail bones are now on display at Dinópolis in Teruel, while visitors in El Castellar can see replicas of the bones unearthed nearby.

articles.title: In 2025, California buried a gas pipeline 20 feet below Alameda Creek and removed its final 8-foot barrier; that same week, Chinook salmon reached this part of the watershed for the first time since the 1950s
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: A barrier that had blocked migratory fish for decades disappeared in California in 2025, and salmon soon followed the newly opened route. Crews reloca.
articles.body: A barrier that had blocked migratory fish for decades disappeared in California in 2025, and salmon soon followed the newly opened route. Crews relocated a Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E) natural-gas pipeline and buried the new section about 20 feet below Alameda Creek near Sunol, then removed the concrete structure that had created an 8-foot drop in the creek. The work reopened more than 20 miles of upstream habitat, and that same week, biologists spotted two Chinook salmon beyond the former barrier, marking the first documented access to this part of the watershed since the 1950s, according to NOAA Fisheries, which reported on the decades-long restoration effort.The barrier that blocked the creekThe pipeline itself was not simply sitting across the creek. It was protected by a concrete erosion-control mat that protruded into the stream channel. That structure created a steep drop that made passage difficult or impossible for migratory fish during most stream flows. The solution was to move the pipeline approximately 100 feet downstream and lower it beneath the creek bed. According to NOAA Fisheries, crews dug a trench about 20 feet deep, installed the new pipeline, removed the old section and its concrete covering, and then reshaped roughly 1,800 feet of the stream channel. The new channel was graded to provide a gradual, more natural passage rather than the previous 8-foot drop.California Trout, which partnered with PG&E on the project, says the pipeline was ultimately lowered approximately 18 feet beneath the creek bed. The difference in the reported depth reflects the descriptions used by the project partners, while the central change remained the same: the pipeline was moved underground deeply enough that the concrete barrier was no longer necessary. NOAA Fisheries provided $4.3 million through its Office of Habitat Conservation for the project. PG&E, Oliver de Silva and a Bay Area foundation contributed additional funding.A 28-year restoration effortThe pipeline project was not an isolated construction job. It was the latest step in a restoration campaign that began in the late 1990s. In 1997, environmentalist Jeff Miller began investigating whether steelhead could be restored to Alameda Creek. He subsequently founded the Alameda Creek Alliance and helped establish the Alameda Creek Fisheries Restoration Workgroup in 1999.At the time, a series of structures had fragmented the creek for migratory fish, including road culverts, water-control dams and other barriers. The last known steelhead sighting in the upper portion of the creek had been in 1967, according to NOAA Fisheries. Yet resident rainbow trout continued to survive in the upper watershed. Scientists later found that some of these fish retained genetic characteristics associated with migratory steelhead, providing another reason to pursue restoration.Over the following decades, agencies, conservation groups and community organisations worked on fish ladders, culvert replacements, dam modifications and other projects. NOAA says partners ultimately opened passage at 18 barriers along Alameda Creek. By 2023, the pipeline-related structure near Sunol was the final major obstacle on the creek's mainstem.More than 20 miles of habitat reopenedRemoving the barrier matters because the upper Alameda Creek watershed contains habitat suitable for spawning and juvenile fish. According to NOAA Fisheries, the restored route gives steelhead access to spawning and juvenile-rearing habitat more than 20 miles upstream, including areas within the Sunol Regional Wilderness. The project also restored natural stream processes in the section where the barrier once stood.California's Department of Fish and Wildlife similarly states that the project was designed to restore access to more than 20 miles of high-quality habitat for migratory fish, including Central California Coast steelhead, Chinook salmon and lamprey species. The restoration also included plans for native vegetation and long-term monitoring.Salmon arrived almost immediatelyThe most remarkable development came in November 2025, when construction had just been completed. Biologists documented two Chinook salmon upstream of the former barrier. NOAA Fisheries identified them as a male and female, while California Trout reported that they were between 12 and 24 inches long. Based on the best available records, the sighting represented the first time salmon had voluntarily accessed this part of the watershed since the 1950s. Claire Buchanan, Central California regional director for California Trout, described the sighting as a sign that the fish were already reclaiming habitat that had been inaccessible for decades. Her comments were reported in California Trout's project announcement following the completion of the work. The return of Chinook does not mean a self-sustaining salmon population has already been established. Scientists and restoration partners are continuing to monitor fish movement and habitat use.Steelhead remain the bigger restoration goalAlthough the Chinook sighting attracted attention, the broader restoration effort is closely tied to threatened Central California Coast steelhead. In February 2026, an Alameda County Water District employee photographed a male and female steelhead moving upstream through a fish ladder in the lower watershed. NOAA Fisheries said they were the first documented adult steelhead independently moving upstream past barriers in that lower section in decades.Scientists are also tracking juvenile rainbow trout moving downstream. Some have been fitted with tags that allow researchers to determine whether they are heading toward the ocean, a journey that could eventually lead to their return as adult steelhead. Restoration partners are monitoring fish, identifying additional priorities and planning projects involving the lower creek, its connection to San Francisco Bay and potential habitat improvements.For Alameda Creek, the buried pipeline therefore represents more than an infrastructure change. It marked the removal of the final major barrier in a nearly three-decade effort to reconnect a fragmented watershed. And within days of that barrier disappearing, salmon provided a striking indication of what the newly opened route could mean for the creek's future.

articles.title: MIT's robotic optics lab built a working laser cavity in 50 maneuvers and under 30 minutes; when researchers moved components, it realigned them automatically with micron-scale precision
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: A robot has assembled a working tabletop laser cavity in less than 30 minutes, handling the precise alignment usually done manually. Massachusetts Ins.
articles.body: A robot has assembled a working tabletop laser cavity in less than 30 minutes, handling the precise alignment usually done manually. Massachusetts Institute of Technology's (MIT's) researchers have developed a reconfigurable robotic optics laboratory that can pick up and position mirrors, lenses and other components, fine-tune them with micron-scale precision and even correct the setup after it is disturbed. According to MIT News, the system successfully assembled a functioning tabletop laser cavity in 50 autonomous manoeuvres within 30 minutes. When researchers deliberately moved components, the robotic system automatically adjusted the setup to maintain the laser's intensity, demonstrating how an autonomous laboratory could continuously monitor and repair its own experiments.A robot takes over the painstaking part of opticsPrecision optics experiments often depend on carefully positioning lasers, mirrors, lenses and cameras. Even a small change in the angle or position of one component can affect the entire experiment, meaning researchers may have to repeatedly adjust and realign equipment.MIT's new system is designed to automate that process from beginning to end. Rather than simply controlling one motorised component, the robotic laboratory can start with optical components that are randomly placed on a tabletop, identify them, move them into position, align them and continuously fine-tune the experiment. It can also dismantle one configuration and build another. The researchers say manual optics experiments can take days or months depending on their complexity. Existing laboratories already use some automated tools, such as motorised systems for adjusting mirrors, but MIT's system combines those functions into a broader autonomous setup. Sachin Vaidya, a postdoctoral researcher at MIT's Research Laboratory of Electronics, said the team's goal was to create a system that could go from no setup to a completely aligned experiment using one automated platform. His comments were reported by MIT News.How the robotic optics lab worksAt the centre of the system is a robotic arm with seven movable joints. It operates on a metallic tabletop and handles optical components housed in specially designed 3D-printed mounts. Each housing carries a QR code containing information about the component inside, including whether it is a mirror or lens and details about its capabilities. Magnetic bases help hold the components securely once they have been placed on the tabletop. The team also developed a wireless fine-adjustment tool that attaches to standard optical mounts. The tool can turn adjustment knobs automatically, allowing the robot to change the angle of a mirror or make similarly precise corrections.Two cameras positioned above the experiment provide a bird's-eye view of the setup. Software then coordinates the different steps, including recognising components, deciding where they need to go, picking them up safely and avoiding collisions. This combination is important because optical experiments are sensitive to extremely small changes. The robot is not simply moving equipment from one location to another; it is also fine-tuning and correcting the experiment as it operates.The 50-manoeuvre laser testTo demonstrate what the system could do, the researchers chose a laser cavity, a component used in many optics experiments. A laser cavity consists of two mirrors positioned on either side of a crystal. Light travels back and forth between the mirrors and passes through the crystal, which amplifies its intensity. Eventually, enough intense light escapes from the system to form a laser. The researchers deliberately selected the laser cavity because it required substantial alignment and optical experience.The robot began with the components unassembled. It then autonomously arranged them into the required configuration and fine-tuned the system. The result was a functioning laser cavity after 50 manoeuvres in less than 30 minutes. That demonstration also showed another capability that could be important for future autonomous laboratories: recovery after disruption.It can correct itself after being disturbedOnce the laser cavity was operating, the researchers deliberately introduced physical disturbances, including randomly moving a component on the tabletop. Instead of requiring a person to inspect the system and manually restore the alignment, the robot detected the change and automatically adjusted the components to maintain the laser's intensity.That self-correction could be particularly useful because optics experiments can be affected by seemingly minor environmental changes. Vibrations or temperature variations can gradually shift components enough to degrade measurements. Vaidya told MIT News that an autonomous system could continuously monitor an experiment and repair its alignment before valuable data is lost.From laboratory experiment to remote scienceMIT researchers envision the system eventually becoming part of a much larger automated research environment. They are developing a cloud-based application that could allow researchers to interact with physical robotic optics laboratories remotely. In the envisioned system, a scientist could submit an experimental protocol or query online, with the robotic laboratory physically assembling and running the requested experiment.The researchers also envision automated systems that could fetch components from a nearby library, deliver them to the optics robot and allow the laboratory to repeatedly build, operate and dismantle different experiments. As MIT News reported, Marin Soljacic, MIT's Cecil and Ida Green Professor of Physics, said such robots could operate continuously without becoming tired or bored, potentially freeing researchers to spend more time developing theories and pursuing new ideas.Potential uses beyond lasersThe technology could eventually be useful far beyond a single laser demonstration. MIT researchers say autonomous optics laboratories could help accelerate testing involving cameras, displays, solar cells and augmented or virtual-reality devices. The team is already applying the robotic lab to research carbon-capture materials. By exposing these materials to light with specific properties, researchers can study how they absorb carbon dioxide. The broader idea is to turn optics from a largely hands-on laboratory process into something that can be assembled, monitored, adjusted and repeated automatically.For now, the MIT system remains a research demonstration, but its 50-manoeuvre laser experiment shows how robotic precision could change the way delicate optical experiments are performed. Instead of spending hours repeatedly adjusting mirrors and lenses, researchers could increasingly leave the alignment, monitoring and even recovery to machines.
